what_it_is.prose: Ilyushin Aviation Complex is Russia's heavy-transport aircraft design bureau (part of the United Aircraft Corporation, under Rostec) and the OEM and design authority for the Indian Air Force's Ilyushin Il-76MD 'Gajraj' — the IAF's Russian-origin four-engine strategic heavy-lifter, of which about 17 were acquired between 1985 and 1989 (roughly 11 to 14 flyable). The Il-76 airframe is doubly important to India because it is the base platform for two key force-multipliers: the six Il-78MKI aerial-refuelling tankers (an Ilyushin derivative) and the three A-50EI 'Phalcon' AWACS, which mount an Israeli EL/W-2090 radar on a Russian Il-76 airframe. The fleet is powered by four Soloviev/Aviadvigatel D-30KP turbofans, and its core challenge is ageing engines and — since the Russia-Ukraine war — disrupted spares and overhaul support, with serviceability reported to have fallen as low as around 32%. India approved an engine-and-avionics modernisation via the Defence Acquisition Council around 2015 (reported ~₹4,250 crore / $650 million) and has studied re-engining with the more efficient Aviadvigatel PS-90A-76, glass-cockpit avionics and indigenous communications — increasingly with domestic firms — to keep a core fleet flying into the 2040s. Ilyushin thus remains a strategically pivotal but war-strained foreign OEM dependency for India's heavy airlift, tanker and AWACS backbone.

faq.question: What is Ilyushin's role for the Indian Air Force?
faq.answer: Ilyushin Aviation Complex (Russia, part of United Aircraft Corporation) is the OEM and design authority for the IAF's Il-76MD 'Gajraj' heavy-lift fleet (~17 acquired 1985–89). The Il-76 airframe also underpins India's six Il-78MKI aerial-refuelling tankers and three A-50EI 'Phalcon' AWACS, making Ilyushin central to India's heavy airlift, tanker and AWACS capabilities.

faq.question: How is India sustaining its ageing Ilyushin Il-76 fleet?
faq.answer: India approved an engine-and-avionics modernisation via the DAC around 2015 (reported ~₹4,250 crore / $650 million) and has studied re-engining with the more efficient Aviadvigatel PS-90A-76 plus glass-cockpit avionics and indigenous communications, increasingly with domestic firms. The aim is to keep a core fleet flying into the 2040s despite Russia-Ukraine-related spares shortages that cut serviceability to as low as ~32%.
